cards.meaning: to lose your footing on a smooth or wet surface
cards.contrast: You SLIP on something smooth — water, oil, polished floor. You TRIP on an obstacle. The cause is the difference.
examples: I slipped on the wet tiles outside the lift.
He slipped and grabbed the railing.

cards.meaning: to move suddenly and unsteadily in one direction
cards.contrast: A LURCH is one violent movement, usually sideways or forward. STAGGERING is several unsteady steps. Vehicles lurch; people stagger.
examples: The bus lurched forward and everyone grabbed something.
He lurched to one side as the train braked.

cards.meaning: to move unsteadily from side to side
cards.contrast: WOBBLING is small and repeated — a table, a cyclist. SWAYING is slower and smoother. STAGGERING involves losing your footing.
examples: The table wobbles because one leg is short.
He wobbled for a second and then got his balance.

cards.meaning: to walk unevenly because one leg hurts
cards.contrast: LIMPING is from pain or injury. HOBBLING is slower and more laboured, often with a stick or with both legs affected.
examples: He limped for a week after the match.
She was limping slightly but said she was fine.

cards.meaning: to walk slowly and without hurry, for pleasure
cards.contrast: STROLLING is relaxed and has direction. WANDERING has no destination. PACING is walking back and forth from nerves.
examples: We strolled back after dinner instead of taking a rickshaw.
He strolled in twenty minutes late.

cards.meaning: to move around without a fixed destination
cards.contrast: WANDERING has no plan. STROLLING is relaxed but going somewhere. Your attention can also wander.
examples: We wandered around the market for an hour.
My mind wandered halfway through the call.

cards.meaning: to walk back and forth repeatedly, usually from stress
cards.contrast: PACING is repetitive and anxious, in a confined space. WANDERING is aimless but calm.
examples: He paced outside the interview room for ten minutes.
She paces when she's on the phone.

cards.meaning: to run a short distance very quickly
cards.contrast: DASHING is short and urgent. SPRINTING is flat-out speed. RUSHING is about being in a hurry, not necessarily running.
examples: I dashed out to catch him before he left.
She dashed across before the signal changed.

cards.meaning: to move quickly with short hurried steps
cards.contrast: SCURRYING is small, quick and slightly panicked — often used for small animals or busy crowds.
examples: Everyone scurried inside when the rain started.
A rat scurried along the wall.

cards.meaning: to push your way in rudely
cards.contrast: BARGING is forceful and rude. SQUEEZING through is careful. PUSHING is neutral — barging implies no apology.
examples: He barged in without knocking.
Someone barged past me at the counter.

cards.meaning: to get through or into a tight space with difficulty
cards.contrast: SQUEEZING is careful and effortful in a narrow gap. BARGING is forceful and rude. You also squeeze a bottle.
examples: I squeezed into the last seat on the bus.
We squeezed past the crowd near the gate.

cards.meaning: to lower your head quickly to avoid something
cards.contrast: DUCKING is fast and downward, to avoid. CROUCHING is deliberate and held. You can also duck out of a meeting.
examples: I ducked under the low doorway.
He ducked out of the call after ten minutes.

cards.meaning: to bend your knees and lower your body, staying on your feet
cards.contrast: CROUCHING keeps you on your feet. KNEELING puts a knee on the ground. SQUATTING is lower, heels down.
examples: He crouched down to pick up the coin.
She crouched behind the counter.

cards.meaning: to drop heavily into a seat or let your posture collapse
cards.contrast: SLUMPING is heavy and tired. LEANING is deliberate and supported. COLLAPSING implies you couldn't stay up at all.
examples: He slumped into the chair and didn't say anything.
Don't slump — it's why your voice sounds tired.

cards.meaning: to sit or lie with your limbs spread out carelessly
cards.contrast: SPRAWLING takes up space, limbs out. SLUMPING is compact and downward.
examples: He was sprawled across two seats, fast asleep.
The papers were sprawled all over the desk.

cards.meaning: to hold something tightly, usually out of fear or need
cards.contrast: CLUTCHING is tight and anxious. HOLDING is neutral. GRABBING is sudden. GRIPPING is firm but calm.
examples: She clutched her bag the whole journey.
He clutched the railing when the bus turned.

cards.meaning: to take something quickly and roughly
cards.contrast: SNATCHING is fast and often without permission. GRABBING is fast but neutral. TAKING is neutral entirely.
examples: He snatched the phone out of my hand.
Someone snatched her chain near the station.

cards.meaning: to pull something suddenly and hard
cards.contrast: YANKING is one sharp pull. TUGGING is repeated and gentler. DRAGGING is slow and continuous.
examples: He yanked the cable out of the wall.
She yanked the door open.

cards.meaning: to pull at something with small repeated movements
cards.contrast: TUGGING is gentle and repeated. YANKING is one hard pull. PULLING is neutral.
examples: The child tugged at his sleeve.
I tugged at the drawer but it wouldn't open.

cards.meaning: to push roughly and suddenly
cards.contrast: SHOVING is rough. NUDGING is gentle and small. PUSHING is neutral in force.
examples: He shoved the box under the desk with his foot.
Someone shoved me from behind in the queue.

cards.meaning: to push gently, often to get attention
cards.contrast: A NUDGE is small and usually with the elbow. A SHOVE is rough. You can also nudge someone about a pending task.
examples: She nudged me when it was my turn to speak.
I'll nudge him about the invoice tomorrow.

cards.meaning: to move something with a quick light movement of a finger
cards.contrast: FLICKING is quick and light — a switch, a crumb, a page. TAPPING is a light touch that stays in place.
examples: He flicked the switch and nothing happened.
She flicked through the report without reading it.

cards.meaning: to search by moving things around untidily
cards.contrast: RUMMAGING is messy and blind — inside a bag or drawer. SEARCHING is neutral. FUMBLING is clumsy handling.
examples: I rummaged through the drawer looking for the charger.
She rummaged in her bag for the keys.

cards.meaning: to spread or throw things in many directions
cards.contrast: SCATTERING spreads things apart. SPILLING is accidental liquid or contents. Crowds also scatter.
examples: The papers scattered when the fan came on.
The crowd scattered as soon as it started raining.

cards.meaning: to let liquid or loose contents fall out accidentally
cards.contrast: SPILLING is accidental. POURING is deliberate. SPLASHING sends it flying.
examples: I spilled chai all over the keyboard.
The bag tore and everything spilled onto the road.

cards.meaning: to make liquid fly about noisily
cards.contrast: SPLASHING is liquid flying with force. SPILLING is liquid escaping. DRIPPING is slow, drop by drop.
examples: A car went past and splashed water all over me.
He splashed cold water on his face.

cards.meaning: to spread something soft or greasy across a surface, messily
cards.contrast: SMEARING spreads and leaves a mark. WIPING removes. SPREADING is neutral and usually deliberate.
examples: He smeared the ink across the page with his sleeve.
There's a smear of oil on the screen.

cards.meaning: to crush something into folds and creases
cards.contrast: CRUMPLING makes irregular creases — paper, cloth. FOLDING is neat. TEARING separates.
examples: He crumpled the receipt and put it in his pocket.
My shirt was crumpled by the time I reached.

cards.meaning: to slide sideways or forward without control
cards.contrast: SKIDDING is uncontrolled sliding, usually vehicles or shoes on a loose surface. SLIPPING is losing footing.
examples: The bike skidded on the gravel.
The car skidded and stopped just short of the wall.

cards.meaning: to knock into something lightly by accident
cards.contrast: BUMPING is light and accidental. CRASHING is heavy. You also bump into people you know.
examples: I bumped my knee on the table leg.
I bumped into an old colleague at the airport.

cards.meaning: to make a series of short knocking sounds
cards.contrast: RATTLING is loose things knocking repeatedly. CREAKING is a slow strained sound. BANGING is one loud impact.
examples: The windows rattle whenever a truck goes past.
Something is rattling inside the drawer.

cards.meaning: to make a long, high sound under strain
cards.contrast: CREAKING is slow and strained — doors, wood, stairs. RATTLING is quick and repeated.
examples: The chair creaks every time I lean back.
The door creaked open on its own.

cards.meaning: to speak unclearly and too quietly to be understood
cards.contrast: MUMBLING is unclear and quiet. MUTTERING is quiet and usually annoyed. SLURRING is running words together.
examples: He mumbled something and looked away.
Don't mumble — nobody at the back can hear you.

cards.meaning: to speak quietly, usually complaining, not meant to be heard
cards.contrast: MUTTERING carries annoyance. MUMBLING is just unclear. WHISPERING is deliberately quiet but clear.
examples: He muttered something about the timing and left.
She was muttering to herself the whole way.

cards.meaning: to say something suddenly, without thinking
cards.contrast: BLURTING is sudden and unplanned, often regretted. INTERRUPTING is about timing, not impulse.
examples: I blurted out the number before checking it.
He blurted it out in front of the whole team.

cards.meaning: to get gradually quieter until you stop speaking
cards.contrast: TRAILING OFF fades out mid-sentence. PAUSING is deliberate and controlled. This is what running out of breath sounds like.
examples: His voice trailed off at the end of every sentence.
She trailed off and looked at her notes.

cards.meaning: to see something for a moment, incompletely
cards.contrast: A GLIMPSE is barely seeing. A GLANCE is deliberately looking briefly. STARING is looking too long.
examples: I only glimpsed the number plate.
We glimpsed the sea between the buildings.

cards.meaning: to look closely with difficulty
cards.contrast: PEERING is effortful — poor light, small print, distance. STARING is easy but too long. GLANCING is quick.
examples: He peered at the screen without his glasses.
She peered through the gap in the curtains.

cards.meaning: to look over something quickly for what you need
cards.contrast: SCANNING is fast and searching. SKIMMING is fast reading for the gist. STUDYING is slow and thorough.
examples: I scanned the list for my name.
He scanned the room and found a seat.

cards.meaning: to stay close by, waiting and slightly in the way
cards.contrast: HOVERING is staying near someone awkwardly. WAITING is neutral. LOITERING implies you shouldn't be there.
examples: The waiter hovered near the table the whole meal.
He hovered outside the cabin until she looked up.
